raw_case_text: A 42-year-old man presented with a six-month history of nonbloody diarrhea associated with the clinical triad of fever, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Anti-Leishmania antibodies serological tests (indirect immunofluorescence title 1 : 640 and rapid test with the recombinant k39) were positive. The diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis was firmed by the detection of amastigotes in a bone marrow aspirate smears. Because of upper gastrointestinal symptoms (mild dysphagia and vomiting), an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed, revealing in duodenum the presence of erosions coated with fibrin, plates of enanthema, and thickened pleats with small whitish spots distributed diffusely. In a tissue fragment obtained by biopsy, the duodenal mucosa showed villous enlarged and filled with numerous histiocytes packed with intracytoplasmic round structures with morphology suggestive of amastigotes of Leishmania spp. The patient received liposomal amphotericin B, 4 mg/kg of body weight during 5 days with complete improvement of visceromegaly, fever and recovery of white blood cell and platelets counts. After treatment and hospital discharge, diarrhea and anemia persisted, and his condition continued to deteriorate. Four months later the patient was admitted once again to hospital with worsening diarrhea, dehydration, metabolic acidosis, and electrolyte imbalance. Blood tests revealed a normochromic normocytic anemia, profound hipoalbuminemia (1.9 g/dL), and a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (120 mm/1 hour). Laboratory examinations also revealed low serum folic acid and iron levels. Both vitamins were replaced and nutritional support was beginning. This time, an extensive search for parasites in stool microscopy was done and eggs of S. mansoni were identified on stool microscopy. The patient was treated with praziquantel 60 mg/kg of body weight. After four weeks, diarrhea remained unchanged, and his condition continued to deteriorate with anorexia and weight loss. Abdominal computer tomography showed mild splenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, and a normal liver size. There was mild dilatation of intestinal loops of the colon. A bone marrow aspiration was also performed showing only reactive changes and no Leishmania amastigotes. Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) assessment on whole blood and bone marrow samples showed positive results using the ribosomal RNA small subunit gene (SSU rRNA) from Leishmania spp. as DNA target. Patient's lymphocyte counts were TCD4+: 539/mm3, TCD8+: 503/mm3 e TCD3+: 1,094/mm3. A colonoscopy was normal. Despite the absence of symptoms of upper gastrointestinal system, an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed, and it showed the presence of diffuse pallor in stomach and duodenum with swollen appearance without ulceration. Duodenal mucosa histopathology showed the persistence of amastigotes, as four months before (Figure 1). The immunohistochemical study confirmed the presence of numerous immunolabeled amastigotes forms of Leishmania (Figure 2). Tests to detect anti-Trypanosoma cruzi antibodies, a protozoan also endemic in Brazil and with tropism for the gastrointestinal tract, and the anti-HIV testing were negative. The patient was treated with amphotericin B deoxycholate, 0.8 mg/kg of body weight for 30 days, and diarrhea resolved completely within two weeks. Two months after the end of treatment the patient had reached its normal weight and normalized erythrocyte levels. The plasmatic levels of IFN-gamma and IL-10 were measured before and after treatment by sandwich-enzyme-linked immuonosorbent assay, as previously described. The results were expressed as picograms per milliliter (pg/mL) based on a standard curve. IFN-gamma was undetectable before and after treatment, while IL-10 levels decreased from 36 pg/mL at initial evaluation to 16.3 pg/mL (55% reduction) after amphotericin treatment and clinical improvement.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presented with persistent worsening nonbloody diarrhea, dehydration, and weight loss 4 months following treatment for visceral leishmaniasis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient originally presented 10 months prior with a 6-month history of nonbloody diarrhea, fever, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, dysphagia, and vomiting. He received a 5-day course of liposomal amphotericin B (4 mg/kg/day) with resolution of fever and cytopenias, but diarrhea and anemia persisted. Four months later, he was readmitted with severe chronic diarrhea, profound dehydration, metabolic acidosis, and progressive cachexia. A course of praziquantel for coinfection produced no improvement in diarrhea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Treated visceral leishmaniasis 4 months prior with liposomal amphotericin B (4 mg/kg for 5 days). Schistosoma mansoni intestinal coinfection treated with praziquantel (60 mg/kg). Country of residence: Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports intractable nonbloody watery diarrhea, dehydration, anorexia, significant weight loss, mild dysphagia, and postprandial vomiting; denies current fevers.

objective.physical_examination: Patient appeared dehydrated and malnourished with metabolic distress. Abdominal examination revealed mild splenomegaly without hepatomegaly or peripheral lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count revealed normocytic normochromic anemia. Serum albumin: 1.9 g/dL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 120 mm/1 hour; low serum folic acid and ferritin/iron levels. T-lymphocyte subsets: CD4+ count 539/mm^3, CD8+ count 503/mm^3, CD3+ count 1,094/mm^3. Stool microscopy: positive for Schistosoma mansoni ova. Anti-Trypanosoma cruzi antibodies: negative. HIV serology: negative. Cytokines: plasma IFN-gamma was undetectable; IL-10 level was 36 pg/mL (decreasing to 16.3 pg/mL post-treatment).
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT scan: mild splenomegaly with normal liver size and no lymphadenopathy; mild dilatation of colonic loops. Initial bone marrow aspirate: reactive changes without intracellular organisms on light microscopy. Colonoscopy: normal colonic mucosa. Upper endoscopy (EGD): diffuse mucosal pallor and swollen appearance of the gastric and duodenal mucosa without ulceration. Duodenal mucosal biopsy: enlarged intestinal villi packed with histiocytic infiltrates containing intracellular protozoa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) targeting the Leishmania small subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU rRNA) gene was positive in whole blood and bone marrow aspirate. Repeat duodenal mucosal biopsy and immunohistochemistry demonstrated abundant immunolabeled Leishmania amastigotes within lamina propria histiocytes, confirming persistent gastrointestinal mucosal leishmaniasis. Anti-Leishmania rK39 rapid test and indirect immunofluorescence (titer 1:640) were positive. Chagas disease, HIV, and intestinal schistosomiasis (eradicated with praziquantel) excluded as causes of persistent diarrhea. Management and Outcome: Nutritional rehabilitation and electrolyte/acidosis correction were initiated with folic acid and iron supplementation. Re-treated with amphotericin B deoxycholate at 0.8 mg/kg/day for 30 days. Diarrhea resolved completely within 2 weeks of therapy initiation. At 2-month post-treatment follow-up, the patient regained baseline body weight and normalized hemoglobin and erythrocyte levels.
